{"id":"COR-2182","uuid":"b88ecb45-eabc-4068-9b73-887e9f4f576a","title":"Distill spends ~75% of wall time in a serial per-checkpoint `git cat-file` scan before the engine starts","description":"## Problem

On the entire-brain repo (2,095 checkpoints, 273 sessions), a full `entire brain distill --force` spends \~42s of a 57s run before `runDistillForBrain` starts. The user sees the "distill sessions" header and then silence; `--json total_seconds` never includes this time because the timer starts inside the engine.

A goroutine dump 20s into the silent phase shows the main goroutine in:

```
runDistill.func3 (distill_cmd.go:811)
→ newEntityProvenanceResolver
→ loadEntityIndexView → finish() → sessionIDsByCheckpoint
→ loadLocalCheckpointSnapshotLocalOnly → loadLocalCheckpointUnionSnapshot
→ readCheckpointSnapshotMetadata → checkpointBlobReader.read
→ catFileWithPolicy → runCheckpointGitLocal → exec.Cmd.Wait
```

It reads each checkpoint's `metadata.json` blob from `refs/heads/entire/checkpoints/v1` with one `git cat-file` subprocess per blob, each preceded by a `git config -z` subprocess. A git-exec shim measured a flat \~34 reads/s for the whole phase: \~2,200 cat-files, \~4,400 process spawns, \~29ms per serialized read.

## Measurements (2026-10-19, M-series mac, deterministic command agent, jobs 4)

| run | wall | pre-engine | engine (`total_seconds`) | git cat-file calls |
| -- | -- | -- | -- | -- |
| distill, materialized transcripts | 57s | \~42s | 15.4s | \~2,200 |
| distill, checkpoint-backed transcripts (<issue id="8f5bc597-0a46-44ee-8e3a-32609cab134a" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2128/entire-brain-remove-the-local-transcript-cache-read-transcripts-from">COR-2128</issue>) | 76s | \~49s | 27.4s | \~2,772 |
| `refresh sessions` (checkpoint-backed export) | 94s | — | — | \~2,486 |

* The scan repeats on every distill run, warm or cold: the entity-index cache can hit, but `loadEntityIndexView.finish()` re-runs the session join unconditionally.
* <issue id="8f5bc597-0a46-44ee-8e3a-32609cab134a" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2128/entire-brain-remove-the-local-transcript-cache-read-transcripts-from">COR-2128</issue> checkpoint-backed brains pay the same per-blob exec pattern again for transcript reads (engine time 15s → 27s, extraction wait 2.2s → 3.9s) and a third time in `refresh sessions`.
* The phase holds the distill pass lock and emits no progress.
* Released nightly and main perform identically; this is not a regression.

## Fix candidates (impact order)

1. Route checkpoint blob reads through one long-lived `git cat-file --batch` process instead of one exec per blob. The blobs are small JSON; batched, this phase should drop from \~42s to well under a second. Applies to the provenance join, the transcript store, and export alike.
2. Cache the per-checkpoint metadata join keyed by the `entire/checkpoints/v1` tip. Checkpoint content is immutable and content-addressed, so the cache never invalidates mid-branch.
3. Drop the `git config -z` preflight per call (halves spawns even without batching).
4. Add a progress line for the phase and include it in `total_seconds` so the cost is visible in the field.

## Repro

Benchmark harness and artifacts: `/tmp/distill-bench/` (isolated `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_*_DIR`, APFS-cloned brain store, deterministic agent `benchmarks/agent-brain/evidence/distill-perf/local-command-agent.py`). Goroutine dump: `GOTRACEBACK=all` + SIGQUIT \~20s into a run. Brain facts: `architecture.distill.bottleneck`.

**Ticket filed and the headline fix is implemented and validated — 82.7s → 17.0s on the same benchmark.**

- **[COR-2182](https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2182/distill-spends-75percent-of-wall-time-in-a-serial-per-checkpoint-git)** (Core, High, assigned to you, In Progress; auto-linked to COR-2128) — full write-up: evidence, stack trace, measurements, fix candidates, and the validated result.

content.text:
{"id":"COR-2182","uuid":"b88ecb45-eabc-4068-9b73-887e9f4f576a","title":"Distill spends ~75% of wall time in a serial per-checkpoint `git cat-file` scan before the engine starts","description":"## Problem

On the entire-brain repo (2,095 checkpoints, 273 sessions), a full `entire brain distill --force` spends \~42s of a 57s run before `runDistillForBrain` starts. The user sees the "distill sessions" header and then silence; `--json total_seconds` never includes this time because the timer starts inside the engine.

A goroutine dump 20s into the silent phase shows the main goroutine in:

```
runDistill.func3 (distill_cmd.go:811)
→ newEntityProvenanceResolver
→ loadEntityIndexView → finish() → sessionIDsByCheckpoint
→ loadLocalCheckpointSnapshotLocalOnly → loadLocalCheckpointUnionSnapshot
→ readCheckpointSnapshotMetadata → checkpointBlobReader.read
→ catFileWithPolicy → runCheckpointGitLocal → exec.Cmd.Wait
```

It reads each checkpoint's `metadata.json` blob from `refs/heads/entire/checkpoints/v1` with one `git cat-file` subprocess per blob, each preceded by a `git config -z` subprocess. A git-exec shim measured a flat \~34 reads/s for the whole phase: \~2,200 cat-files, \~4,400 process spawns, \~29ms per serialized read.

## Measurements (2026-10-19, M-series mac, deterministic command agent, jobs 4)

| run | wall | pre-engine | engine (`total_seconds`) | git cat-file calls |
| -- | -- | -- | -- | -- |
| distill, materialized transcripts | 57s | \~42s | 15.4s | \~2,200 |
| distill, checkpoint-backed transcripts (<issue id="8f5bc597-0a46-44ee-8e3a-32609cab134a" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2128/entire-brain-remove-the-local-transcript-cache-read-transcripts-from">COR-2128</issue>) | 76s | \~49s | 27.4s | \~2,772 |
| `refresh sessions` (checkpoint-backed export) | 94s | — | — | \~2,486 |

* The scan repeats on every distill run, warm or cold: the entity-index cache can hit, but `loadEntityIndexView.finish()` re-runs the session join unconditionally.
* <issue id="8f5bc597-0a46-44ee-8e3a-32609cab134a" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2128/entire-brain-remove-the-local-transcript-cache-read-transcripts-from">COR-2128</issue> checkpoint-backed brains pay the same per-blob exec pattern again for transcript reads (engine time 15s → 27s, extraction wait 2.2s → 3.9s) and a third time in `refresh sessions`.
* The phase holds the distill pass lock and emits no progress.

content.text:
**Different cache entirely — and I've now tested the cold path directly.**

**Q1: Was the 17s result a warm first run?** The 82.7s→17.0s comparison had a warm *metadata* cache (the brain had been exported before). I just reran the patched binary with the cache file deleted: **80.8s, ~2,200 cat-files — the full old behavior comes back** (output still identical). So the speedup depends entirely on that cache. That's safe for a true first-time run, though: distill refuses to run until sessions are exported, and the sessions export itself builds and saves this cache (`export.go:177–199`; my fresh isolated env confirmed `refresh sessions` created it). So a new machine pays the blob scan **once, in export** (the 94s I measured), and every distill after that reads the cache. The only way distill goes cold is a pre-cache-era brain or manually deleting the file, and then it degrades to the old scan, not an error.

**Q2: Relation to the removed transcript cache — different caches:**

- **Transcript cache (removed by COR-2128):** the 1.6GB of materialized `full.jsonl` *content* files under `<brain>/sessions/`. Gone; transcripts now stream from git checkpoint refs on demand.
- **Checkpoint metadata cache (what my fix uses):** `export/checkpoint-metadata-cache.json.gz`, ~2.7MB gzip'd, OID-keyed copies of each checkpoint's small `metadata.json` (session membership, timestamps). It survived COR-2128 — in fact COR-2128 made it *more* load-bearing, because the transcript store resolves session→checkpoint locations through this same cache (`transcript_store.go:233`). My fix just gives the distill provenance join the same cache the transcript store and export already use.

What remains uncached is transcript **content**. On the checkpoint-backed brain the patched binary runs 33.0s: pre-engine drops to ~1s, but 572 `cat-file` calls remain — those are the actual transcript chunk reads. Caching those would just reintroduce the transcript cache COR-2128 deleted; the right fix there (and for the export-side first scan) is one long-lived `git cat-file --batch` process instead of a subprocess per blob. Both validation rows are appended to COR-2182.

I'm planning a sweep across corpus sizes—from an empty user with zero sessions up through the full 273 sessions/2095 checkpoints—comparing the old materialized-transcript brain, the current git-backed brain, and the post-fix version to see how performance scales.

For a genuinely new user, there's no metadata cache yet, so the realistic flow is to run `refresh sessions` from scratch (building the cache and paying the scan cost) followed by distill. That means the after-fix config gets to benefit from the freshly built cache during distill, while the before-fix configs still re-scan regardless—this gives an honest comparison of first-run behavior rather than an artificial no-cache worst case for everyone.

For generating corpora of varying size, I'm thinking about truncating the real repo's checkpoint branch, since resetting that ref to an older ancestor commit naturally gives fewer checkpoints and proportionally fewer sessions, letting me scale the corpus size by picking different ancestor commits.

For materialized-transcript brains, I need the old pre-COR-2128 binary since current builds use checkpoint-backed storage, so I'd have to check out and build from before that commit merged to produce comparable old-mode brains at each corpus size.

Mixing binaries across the three configs gets confusing, so I'm trying to simplify: old brain = materialized transcripts via pre-fix binary, current brain = checkpoint-backed on main-before-fix, new brain = checkpoint-backed with the patch applied. Given the effort involved, I'm leaning toward a more pragmatic approach since the dominant costs scale mechanically and linearly with checkpoint count anyway.

Actually, I realize truncating the brain itself won't reduce the checkpoint scan cost, since that scan operates against the git repo's checkpoint count rather than the brain's session data — so pruning the materialized brain wouldn't help simulate smaller sizes for that part of the cost.

So the real plan is to create scratch clones of the repo and adjust the checkpoint ref to point at ancestor commits yielding different checkpoint counts (0, ~500, ~1000, 2095), while keeping the main history constant across sizes since it doesn't affect the sweep.

For 0 checkpoints, deleting the ref entirely simulates a brand-new user: export would produce an empty manifest and distill would essentially no-op, giving a near-zero baseline measuring just CLI overhead.

For each checkpoint size, I need to test multiple configs: the unfixed binary doing refresh+distill, the fixed binary doing the same, and the old materialized-export path using a pre-COR-2128 binary to export then distilling with the current main binary, which mirrors the scenario I'd already been using as my template.

To build that pre-fix binary I'd check out the parent of the COR-2128 commit. To pick commits with roughly 500 and 1000 checkpoints, I can count distinct checkpoint directories (two-level path prefixes) in a tree listing at various commits along history, then use whatever actual session counts come out of the export manifest as the real sizes to report. For runtime, I can extrapolate roughly linearly from the full export time of 94 seconds down to smaller fractions for half and quarter sizes, then account for distill time separately.

Overall across all sizes and configs this amounts to maybe 15-20 minutes of total machine time, which seems acceptable to run sequentially in the background. The trickier question is the cache assumption: the user wants me to assume no metadata cache exists, but in the real pipeline, refreshing sessions builds that cache before distill runs, so the "no cache" scenario doesn't naturally occur once export has happened. I'm leaning toward reporting the honest pipeline as it really behaves, plus an extra column showing the cache-deleted case for completeness.

I'm settling on three clean cells per size: old materialized export feeding the unfixed distill, new git-backed export feeding the unfixed distill, and new git-backed export feeding the fixed distill, since the export code itself doesn't change with the fix.

I should also add a worst-case column — running the fixed distill with its cache file deleted, effectively reproducing pre-fix behavior cheaply at every size rather than just at full scale.

For binaries, I'm double-checking that entire-brain-prof was built before my patch (so it represents unfixed main) and entire-brain-fixed was built afterward from the patched tree, confirming the prof binary hasn't changed since.

For the pre-COR-2128 comparison, I'll build from the commit before fcdaf8bb (the #391 merge) using `git worktree add` at its first parent, in a separate temp directory so I don't disturb the current dirty worktree with my uncommitted fix. Now thinking about checkpoint ref truncation: I need to clone the repo into a temp path for each size variant, making sure the checkpoint branch and full main history come along. Since the worktree shares .git with the main repo, cloning locally from it should pull refs/heads including the checkpoint branch, but refs outside refs/heads (like refs/entire/checkpoints) won't come along automatically, so I need to account for that when setting up the clone.

I'm also weighing whether removing origin entirely breaks repo-key derivation since that depends on the remote URL — probably fine to fall back to path-based keying since it stays consistent within each isolated test cell. import subprocess
revs = subprocess.run(['git','rev-list','refs/heads/entire/checkpoints/v1'],capture_output=True,text=True).stdout.split()
print('total commits on v1:', len(revs))
import re
def count(c):
    out = subprocess.run(['git','ls-tree','-r','-d','--name-only',c],capture_output=True,text=True).stdout
    return sum(1 for l in out.splitlines() if re.fullmatch(r'..\/[^/]+', l))
# sample to find ~500 and ~1000
targets={500:None,1000:None}
lo_count=count(revs[-1]); hi_count=count(revs[0])
print('newest tree checkpoints:', hi_count, 'oldest:', lo_count)
# binary search per target over position in rev list (older = higher index)
import bisect
def count_at(i): return count(revs[i])
for t in targets:
    lo, hi = 0, len(revs)-1   # lo=newest(max), hi=oldest(min)
    while lo < hi-1:
        mid=(lo+hi)//2
        if count_at(mid) >= t: lo=mid
        else: hi=mid
    targets[t]=(revs[lo], count_at(lo))
for t,(c,n) in targets.items(): print(f'target {t}: {c[:12]} actual={n}')
EOF

With the full dataset in, I'm assembling the sweep table — the distill-nocache run at 1007 took 162.7s, notably slower than B's 96.9s since forcing a re-distill on a git-backed brain means no metadata cache, so it pays for the full scan, git transcript reads, and reconciling against 326 existing facts; I'm flagging it as the worst case. Fact counts stay consistent across configs per size (155/213/326), confirming determinism.

Now checking the smaller sizes: at 250 and 500, the nocache distill numbers look oddly close to the cached distill times (12.8 vs 13.4, 17.3 vs 17.7), and at 500 the nocache run is even faster than B's cached run (17.3 vs 47.3), which seems off — I'd expect the forced rescan to add real overhead there, so something about how the cache deletion and --force rerun interact at smaller sizes needs more scrutiny.

I'm puzzled by the non-monotonic timing in sweep C-nocache—250/500 checkpoints ran fast but 1007 was slow, which doesn't fit a simple "scan repeats every run" explanation. I'm considering whether the template clone's brainDir already had entity data baked in, versus whether something about checkpoint snapshot resolution or distill fingerprint caching behaves differently depending on checkpoint count.

Checking whether the provenance resolver bails out early when the entity index is empty, since that could explain why the measured time came in well under the expected scan-plus-engine total—tracing through whether the checkpoint-to-session join actually executes before or after that early-exit check.

But that still doesn't explain the B vs C discrepancy: if the pre-engine provenance scan was skipped entirely for both environments due to empty gitmeta cache, the slowdown in B's distill times must come from somewhere else in the pipeline, not the provenance resolution step I was focused on.

Wait, I need to reconsider — in the earlier goroutine dump from the isolated environment with template data and empty cache dir, the main goroutine was actually inside the provenance join path. So the join does execute despite an empty gitmeta cache, which means my assumption that OpenMetaStore fails silently on an empty tip isn't quite right — I need to check whether the store errors out on a missing directory versus just returning an empty tip, since that determines whether the resolver gets skipped or not.

Looking closer, the brain directory contains a persisted entity index cache file that the template environment populates with entries. So loadEntityIndexCache finds hasPrevious=true, and the tip comparison between the previous cached tip and the current (likely empty) tip triggers a mismatch, forcing a rebuild from an empty gitmeta state — which should produce an empty cache. But the dump clearly showed the finish/join callback running afterward, so finish must be getting called on both the cache-hit path and the post-rebuild path, regardless of whether the rebuilt cache ends up empty.

Tracing the rebuild path: once rebuild succeeds, the code assigns the new cache to view.cache, checks for migration needs, then falls through to call finish(). Critically, finish() runs sessionIDsByCheckpoint unconditionally — it doesn't check entry count first. Only afterward does newEntityProvenanceResolver check Entries==0 and bail out, returning nil. So the expensive scan happens and gets paid for even though the result is immediately discarded.

That explains why the scan ran in template environments despite an empty gitmeta and empty rebuilt cache — finish() just does the join scan regardless. Now I need to check whether SWEEP environments, which start from fresh brains with no entities/index.json file present at all, hit this same wasteful path.

Looking at the timing data though: B-1007's 96.9s matches the full pre-fix behavior with both scan and engine time, so the scan clearly ran there too. C-1007's 31.5s looks like engine-only time, suggesting the scan was skipped or served from the metadata cache. But C-nocache-1007 at 162.7s is much larger — running without cache, forced, with 326 existing facts to reconcile — which is consistent with the scan running in sweep environments as well, just with added reconciliation overhead.

But the 250/500 timings (12.8s/17.3s) are far too fast for a true no-cache scan at that scale — if the scan actually ran without metadata cache against 500 sessions, I'd expect checkpoint/blob overhead pushing well past 40s, not 17.3s. {"id":"COR-2182","uuid":"b88ecb45-eabc-4068-9b73-887e9f4f576a","title":"Distill spends ~75% of wall time in a serial per-checkpoint `git cat-file` scan before the engine starts","description":"## Problem

On the entire-brain repo (2,095 checkpoints, 273 sessions), a full `entire brain distill --force` spends \~42s of a 57s run before `runDistillForBrain` starts. The user sees the "distill sessions" header and then silence; `--json total_seconds` never includes this time because the timer starts inside the engine.

A goroutine dump 20s into the silent phase shows the main goroutine in:

```
runDistill.func3 (distill_cmd.go:811)
→ newEntityProvenanceResolver
→ loadEntityIndexView → finish() → sessionIDsByCheckpoint
→ loadLocalCheckpointSnapshotLocalOnly → loadLocalCheckpointUnionSnapshot
→ readCheckpointSnapshotMetadata → checkpointBlobReader.read
→ catFileWithPolicy → runCheckpointGitLocal → exec.Cmd.Wait
```

It reads each checkpoint's `metadata.json` blob from `refs/heads/entire/checkpoints/v1` with one `git cat-file` subprocess per blob, each preceded by a `git config -z` subprocess. A git-exec shim measured a flat \~34 reads/s for the whole phase: \~2,200 cat-files, \~4,400 process spawns, \~29ms per serialized read.

## Measurements (2026-10-19, M-series mac, deterministic command agent, jobs 4)

| run | wall | pre-engine | engine (`total_seconds`) | git cat-file calls |
| -- | -- | -- | -- | -- |
| distill, materialized transcripts | 57s | \~42s | 15.4s | \~2,200 |
| distill, checkpoint-backed transcripts (<issue id="8f5bc597-0a46-44ee-8e3a-32609cab134a" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2128/entire-brain-remove-the-local-transcript-cache-read-transcripts-from">COR-2128</issue>) | 76s | \~49s | 27.4s | \~2,772 |
| `refresh sessions` (checkpoint-backed export) | 94s | — | — | \~2,486 |

* The scan repeats on every distill run, warm or cold: the entity-index cache can hit, but `loadEntityIndexView.finish()` re-runs the session join unconditionally.
* <issue id="8f5bc597-0a46-44ee-8e3a-32609cab134a" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2128/entire-brain-remove-the-local-transcript-cache-read-transcripts-from">COR-2128</issue> checkpoint-backed brains pay the same per-blob exec pattern again for transcript reads (engine time 15s → 27s, extraction wait 2.2s → 3.9s) and a third time in `refresh sessions`.
* The phase holds the distill pass lock and emits no progress.
* Released nightly and main perform identically; this is not a regression.

## Fix candidates (impact order)

1. Route checkpoint blob reads through one long-lived `git cat-file --batch` process instead of one exec per blob. The blobs are small JSON; batched, this phase should drop from \~42s to well under a second. Applies to the provenance join, the transcript store, and export alike.
2. Cache the per-checkpoint metadata join keyed by the `entire/checkpoints/v1` tip. Checkpoint content is immutable and content-addressed, so the cache never invalidates mid-branch.
3. Drop the `git config -z` preflight per call (halves spawns even without batching).
4. Add a progress line for the phase and include it in `total_seconds` so the cost is visible in the field.

## Repro

Benchmark harness and artifacts: `/tmp/distill-bench/` (isolated `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_*_DIR`, APFS-cloned brain store, deterministic agent `benchmarks/agent-brain/evidence/distill-perf/local-command-agent.py`). Goroutine dump: `GOTRACEBACK=all` + SIGQUIT \~20s into a run. Brain facts: `architecture.distill.bottleneck`.

## Validated fix (2026-10-19)

`sessionIDsByCheckpoint` (entities_cmd.go:868) passed a nil `*checkpointMetadataCache` to `loadLocalCheckpointSnapshotLocalOnly`, so the provenance join bypassed the export-maintained blob cache (`export/checkpoint-metadata-cache.json.gz`) that the export path and the transcript store already read through. OID resolution is gated on `cache != nil`, so the nil argument also disabled cache lookups downstream.

One-call-site change: load the cache read-only (same pattern as transcript_store.go:233) and pass it.

Same benchmark (git-shim, same template brain, same machine):

|  | before | after |
| -- | -- | -- |
| wall | 82.7s | 17.0s |
| first session done | 67.1s | 2.6s |
| git subprocesses | 4,443 | 53 |
| `git cat-file` calls | \~2,200 | 0 |
| output (facts/chunks/agent calls) | 2590/327/607 | identical |

Focused `internal/cli` tests (Distill/Entit/Provenance/cache/snapshot) pass. Change is uncommitted in the hamburg workspace pending review.

Still open from the candidates list: batched reads (`git cat-file --batch`) for the new-mode transcript path (engine 27.4s vs 15.4s) and the cold `refresh sessions` export (\~2,486 cat-files); progress/timing visibility for pre-engine phases.

## Cache-dependency validation

| patched binary, run | wall | first session done | git cat-file |
| -- | -- | -- | -- |
| metadata cache present (any brain after one export) | 17.0s | 2.6s | 0 |
| metadata cache file deleted | 80.8s | 66.2s | \~2,200 |
| <issue id="8f5bc597-0a46-44ee-8e3a-32609cab134a" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2128/entire-brain-remove-the-local-transcript-cache-read-transcripts-from">COR-2128</issue> checkpoint-backed brain, cache present | 33.0s | 15.0s | 572 (transcript chunks only) |

The speedup depends entirely on `export/checkpoint-metadata-cache.json.gz`. That is safe for the normal flow: distill refuses to run before sessions are exported, and the sessions export loads and saves this cache under the brain write lock (export.go:177-199), so first-time setup pays the blob scan once (in export) and every later distill reads the cache. A missing cache file (pre-cache-era brain, manual deletion) degrades to the old serial scan with identical output.

The remaining 572 cat-files on checkpoint-backed brains are transcript content chunks — the metadata cache does not and should not hold them (that would reintroduce the transcript cache <issue id="8f5bc597-0a46-44ee-8e3a-32609cab134a" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2128/entire-brain-remove-the-local-transcript-cache-read-transcripts-from">COR-2128</issue> removed). Batching via `git cat-file --batch` is the right fix for those and for the export-side first scan.

content.text:
One changed call site in `internal/cli/entities_cmd.go` (`sessionIDsByCheckpoint`, the join distill builds before it starts):

```diff
-	if snapshot, _, err := loadLocalCheckpointSnapshotLocalOnly(..., nil); err == nil && snapshot != nil {
+	metadataCache := loadCheckpointMetadataCache(filepath.Join(brainDir, filepath.FromSlash(checkpointMetadataCachePath)))
+	if snapshot, _, err := loadLocalCheckpointSnapshotLocalOnly(..., metadataCache); err == nil && snapshot != nil {
```

It was passing `nil` where a `*checkpointMetadataCache` belongs. That nil had two effects downstream:

1. The snapshot loader skips OID resolution when the cache is nil, so every checkpoint's `metadata.json` was read with its own `git cat-file` subprocess (~2,200 of them, serially).
2. Even though export maintains a cache of exactly these blobs (`export/checkpoint-metadata-cache.json.gz`, 2.7MB), this path never looked at it.

The fix loads that cache read-only — same pattern the transcript store already uses at `transcript_store.go:233` — and passes it through. Cache hit → blob reads become map lookups; cache miss → falls back to the old per-blob `cat-file` with identical output. Export remains the only writer of the cache file.

content.text:
{"id":"COR-2182","uuid":"b88ecb45-eabc-4068-9b73-887e9f4f576a","title":"Distill spends ~75% of wall time in a serial per-checkpoint `git cat-file` scan before the engine starts","description":"## Problem

On the entire-brain repo (2,095 checkpoints, 273 sessions), a full `entire brain distill --force` spends \~42s of a 57s run before `runDistillForBrain` starts. The user sees the "distill sessions" header and then silence; `--json total_seconds` never includes this time because the timer starts inside the engine.

A goroutine dump 20s into the silent phase shows the main goroutine in:

```
runDistill.func3 (distill_cmd.go:811)
→ newEntityProvenanceResolver
→ loadEntityIndexView → finish() → sessionIDsByCheckpoint
→ loadLocalCheckpointSnapshotLocalOnly → loadLocalCheckpointUnionSnapshot
→ readCheckpointSnapshotMetadata → checkpointBlobReader.read
→ catFileWithPolicy → runCheckpointGitLocal → exec.Cmd.Wait
```

It reads each checkpoint's `metadata.json` blob from `refs/heads/entire/checkpoints/v1` with one `git cat-file` subprocess per blob, each preceded by a `git config -z` subprocess. A git-exec shim measured a flat \~34 reads/s for the whole phase: \~2,200 cat-files, \~4,400 process spawns, \~29ms per serialized read.

## Measurements (2026-10-19, M-series mac, deterministic command agent, jobs 4)

| run | wall | pre-engine | engine (`total_seconds`) | git cat-file calls |
| -- | -- | -- | -- | -- |
| distill, materialized transcripts | 57s | \~42s | 15.4s | \~2,200 |
| distill, checkpoint-backed transcripts (<issue id="8f5bc597-0a46-44ee-8e3a-32609cab134a" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2128/entire-brain-remove-the-local-transcript-cache-read-transcripts-from">COR-2128</issue>) | 76s | \~49s | 27.4s | \~2,772 |
| `refresh sessions` (checkpoint-backed export) | 94s | — | — | \~2,486 |

* The scan repeats on every distill run, warm or cold: the entity-index cache can hit, but `loadEntityIndexView.finish()` re-runs the session join unconditionally.
* <issue id="8f5bc597-0a46-44ee-8e3a-32609cab134a" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2128/entire-brain-remove-the-local-transcript-cache-read-transcripts-from">COR-2128</issue> checkpoint-backed brains pay the same per-blob exec pattern again for transcript reads (engine time 15s → 27s, extraction wait 2.2s → 3.9s) and a third time in `refresh sessions`.
* The phase holds the distill pass lock and emits no progress.
* Released nightly and main perform identically; this is not a regression.

## Fix candidates (impact order)

1. Route checkpoint blob reads through one long-lived `git cat-file --batch` process instead of one exec per blob. The blobs are small JSON; batched, this phase should drop from \~42s to well under a second. Applies to the provenance join, the transcript store, and export alike.
2. Cache the per-checkpoint metadata join keyed by the `entire/checkpoints/v1` tip. Checkpoint content is immutable and content-addressed, so the cache never invalidates mid-branch.
3. Drop the `git config -z` preflight per call (halves spawns even without batching).
4. Add a progress line for the phase and include it in `total_seconds` so the cost is visible in the field.

## Repro

Benchmark harness and artifacts: `/tmp/distill-bench/` (isolated `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_*_DIR`, APFS-cloned brain store, deterministic agent `benchmarks/agent-brain/evidence/distill-perf/local-command-agent.py`). Goroutine dump: `GOTRACEBACK=all` + SIGQUIT \~20s into a run. Brain facts: `architecture.distill.bottleneck`.

## Validated fix (2026-10-19)

`sessionIDsByCheckpoint` (entities_cmd.go:868) passed a nil `*checkpointMetadataCache` to `loadLocalCheckpointSnapshotLocalOnly`, so the provenance join bypassed the export-maintained blob cache (`export/checkpoint-metadata-cache.json.gz`) that the export path and the transcript store already read through. OID resolution is gated on `cache != nil`, so the nil argument also disabled cache lookups downstream.

One-call-site change: load the cache read-only (same pattern as transcript_store.go:233) and pass it.

Same benchmark (git-shim, same template brain, same machine):

|  | before | after |
| -- | -- | -- |
| wall | 82.7s | 17.0s |
| first session done | 67.1s | 2.6s |
| git subprocesses | 4,443 | 53 |
| `git cat-file` calls | \~2,200 | 0 |
| output (facts/chunks/agent calls) | 2590/327/607 | identical |

Focused `internal/cli` tests (Distill/Entit/Provenance/cache/snapshot) pass. Change is uncommitted in the hamburg workspace pending review.

Still open from the candidates list: batched reads (`git cat-file --batch`) for the new-mode transcript path (engine 27.4s vs 15.4s) and the cold `refresh sessions` export (\~2,486 cat-files); progress/timing visibility for pre-engine phases.

## Cache-dependency validation

| patched binary, run | wall | first session done | git cat-file |
| -- | -- | -- | -- |

On the entire-brain repo (2,095 checkpoints, 273 sessions), a full `entire brain distill --force` spends \~42s of a 57s run before `runDistillForBrain` starts. The user sees the "distill sessions" header and then silence; `--json total_seconds` never includes this time because the timer starts inside the engine.

A goroutine dump 20s into the silent phase shows the main goroutine in:

```
runDistill.func3 (distill_cmd.go:811)
→ newEntityProvenanceResolver
→ loadEntityIndexView → finish() → sessionIDsByCheckpoint
→ loadLocalCheckpointSnapshotLocalOnly → loadLocalCheckpointUnionSnapshot
→ readCheckpointSnapshotMetadata → checkpointBlobReader.read
→ catFileWithPolicy → runCheckpointGitLocal → exec.Cmd.Wait
```

It reads each checkpoint's `metadata.json` blob from `refs/heads/entire/checkpoints/v1` with one `git cat-file` subprocess per blob, each preceded by a `git config -z` subprocess. A git-exec shim measured a flat \~34 reads/s for the whole phase: \~2,200 cat-files, \~4,400 process spawns, \~29ms per serialized read.

Entire MCP — an investigation surface over Entire's engineering data: repos and their analytics, git history (commits, files, trees, refs, diffs), the AI checkpoints and sessions behind the code (with transcripts and token accounting), trails (PR-like change proposals), and code search. Reads are curated `*_entire` tools; a small write/ops group covers trail/review/runner/dispatch mutations.

Workflow: when you only have a repo name, path, or URL, call resolve_entire_repo first, then pass the repo it returns to repo-scoped tools. Prefer the aggregation tools (get_entire_repo_overview, get_entire_my_activity) over hand-rolling stats from raw listings.

Querying conventions (shared by every tool):
- Addressing: name a repo by a prefixed path (gh/<owner>/<repo>, et/<project>/<repo>, git/<owner>/<repo>) or a repo ULID. Repo ULIDs are REGION-SCOPED — the same repo has a different ULID per region, so never carry a ULID across regions or sessions; if a tool rejects one, re-resolve with resolve_entire_repo.
- Pagination: every list takes an opaque cursor and returns next_cursor when more remains — exhaust the pages before concluding "that's all".
- Time: since/until are ISO 8601 / RFC3339 bounds; where offered, timeframe is a relative window (last-month, last-3-months, last-6-months).
- Size: reads that can be large (files, diffs, transcripts) honor max_tokens and return next_cursor to continue — raise max_tokens or page rather than assuming truncation is the whole story.

Pitfalls:
- sessions[].tokenUsage on a checkpoint is a PER-CHECKPOINT delta, not a session total — sum across a session's checkpoints, or use get_entire_session for the authoritative total.
- list_entire_checkpoints silently truncates older history; for a branch's COMPLETE checkpoint membership, paginate list_entire_commits and collect the per-commit checkpoint IDs.

Skills: before deep work in a domain, load the matching skill (list_entire_skills / load_entire_skill) — entire/checkpoints-and-sessions and entire/token-analysis before token accounting, … [truncated]

cat > /tmp/distill-bench/baseline.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/zsh
BENCH=/tmp/distill-bench
D=$BENCH/runs/baseline-main
rm -rf $D; mkdir -p $D/{data,state,cache,config}
cd $BENCH/sweep/repo-1007
E=(env ENTIRE_PLUGIN_DATA_DIR=$D/data ENTIRE_PLUGIN_STATE_DIR=$D/state ENTIRE_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR=$D/cache ENTIRE_PLUGIN_CONFIG_DIR=$D/config PATH=$BENCH/shim:$PATH)
now() { python3 -c 'import time;print(time.time())' }
t0=$(now)
GIT_SHIM_LOG=$D/git-export.log $E $BENCH/bin/entire-brain-baseline refresh sessions > $D/export.out 2>&1
t1=$(now)
GIT_SHIM_LOG=$D/git-distill.log $E $BENCH/bin/entire-brain-baseline distill --json --agent command --agent-command python3 --agent-command benchmarks/agent-brain/evidence/distill-perf/local-command-agent.py --max-chunk-bytes 262144 --confidence 0.75 --jobs 4 > $D/distill.json 2> $D/distill.err
t2=$(now)
echo "export_s=$(printf %.1f $((t1-t0))) distill_s=$(printf %.1f $((t2-t1))) total_s=$(printf %.1f $((t2-t0)))"
echo "export git calls: $(wc -l < $D/git-export.log)"; awk '{print $6}' $D/git-export.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3
echo "distill git calls: $(wc -l < $D/git-distill.log)"; awk '{print $6}' $D/git-distill.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3
python3 -c "
import json; r=json.load(open('$D/distill.json'))
print('engine:', {k:round(r[k],1) for k in ('total_seconds','extraction_wait_seconds','reconcile_seconds','write_seconds')}, 'facts:', r['facts'])"
echo BASELINE-DONE
EOF
chmod +x /tmp/distill-bench/baseline.sh && /tmp/distill-bench/baseline.sh

The per-call `config -z` is actually `enumerateRepoFilterDrivers`, a filter-driver probe running before protected git commands—and it fires 2,501 times in the export, once per git call. The "must not enter the cache" comment implies a cache exists but failures bypass it, yet the 1:1 config-to-cat-file ratio suggests caching isn't happening in this flow at all, which is itself worth flagging as a finding.

I have enough to write up the deliverable now. The mechanism walks roughly 1,007 checkpoints via tree listings, reading metadata.json through a cold-cache path into cat-file calls with lazy-fetch disabled.

The real cost driver is clear: nearly 5,000 serial git subprocess spawns (cat-files plus per-spawn config probes for hardening) account for 98+ seconds of wall time against only a few MB of actual data moved — almost entirely process-spawn overhead rather than I/O, something a single long-lived `git cat-file --batch` process could collapse to under a second. My proposal is to build a `gitBlobBatchReader` that spawns one persistent batch process per git directory with the same hardened environment, feeding it refs or OIDs over stdin and parsing the returned object records, while using `--batch-check` to replace the individual existence-probe calls.

This batch reader should sit at the chokepoint where catFileWithPolicy, transcript validation, and transcript reads all converge, so export, distill, and the transcript store all inherit the speedup from one implementation. I also want to amortize the filter-driver enumeration to run once per repo/process instead of thousands of times, and build in safety: no network subcommands needed since this is cat-file only, kill the child on context cancellation, cap response sizes, and fall back to the per-exec path if the batch process fails. This should bring export time down from 98s to roughly 15-25s, with the remaining overhead coming from other git calls like ls-tree.

Distill should drop from 38s to about 22s since the 570 transcript reads collapse into the batch, bringing total cold first-run time from 136s to roughly 40-50s. {"id":"COR-2182","uuid":"b88ecb45-eabc-4068-9b73-887e9f4f576a","title":"Distill spends ~75% of wall time in a serial per-checkpoint `git cat-file` scan before the engine starts","description":"## Problem

On the entire-brain repo (2,095 checkpoints, 273 sessions), a full `entire brain distill --force` spends \~42s of a 57s run before `runDistillForBrain` starts. The user sees the "distill sessions" header and then silence; `--json total_seconds` never includes this time because the timer starts inside the engine.

A goroutine dump 20s into the silent phase shows the main goroutine in:

```
runDistill.func3 (distill_cmd.go:811)
→ newEntityProvenanceResolver
→ loadEntityIndexView → finish() → sessionIDsByCheckpoint
→ loadLocalCheckpointSnapshotLocalOnly → loadLocalCheckpointUnionSnapshot
→ readCheckpointSnapshotMetadata → checkpointBlobReader.read
→ catFileWithPolicy → runCheckpointGitLocal → exec.Cmd.Wait
```

It reads each checkpoint's `metadata.json` blob from `refs/heads/entire/checkpoints/v1` with one `git cat-file` subprocess per blob, each preceded by a `git config -z` subprocess. A git-exec shim measured a flat \~34 reads/s for the whole phase: \~2,200 cat-files, \~4,400 process spawns, \~29ms per serialized read.

## Measurements (2026-10-19, M-series mac, deterministic command agent, jobs 4)

| run | wall | pre-engine | engine (`total_seconds`) | git cat-file calls |
| -- | -- | -- | -- | -- |
| distill, materialized transcripts | 57s | \~42s | 15.4s | \~2,200 |
| distill, checkpoint-backed transcripts (<issue id="8f5bc597-0a46-44ee-8e3a-32609cab134a" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2128/entire-brain-remove-the-local-transcript-cache-read-transcripts-from">COR-2128</issue>) | 76s | \~49s | 27.4s | \~2,772 |
| `refresh sessions` (checkpoint-backed export) | 94s | — | — | \~2,486 |

* The scan repeats on every distill run, warm or cold: the entity-index cache can hit, but `loadEntityIndexView.finish()` re-runs the session join unconditionally.
* <issue id="8f5bc597-0a46-44ee-8e3a-32609cab134a" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2128/entire-brain-remove-the-local-transcript-cache-read-transcripts-from">COR-2128</issue> checkpoint-backed brains pay the same per-blob exec pattern again for transcript reads (engine time 15s → 27s, extraction wait 2.2s → 3.9s) and a third time in `refresh sessions`.
* The phase holds the distill pass lock and emits no progress.
* Released nightly and main perform identically; this is not a regression.

## Fix candidates (impact order)

1. Route checkpoint blob reads through one long-lived `git cat-file --batch` process instead of one exec per blob. The blobs are small JSON; batched, this phase should drop from \~42s to well under a second. Applies to the provenance join, the transcript store, and export alike.
2. Cache the per-checkpoint metadata join keyed by the `entire/checkpoints/v1` tip. Checkpoint content is immutable and content-addressed, so the cache never invalidates mid-branch.
3. Drop the `git config -z` preflight per call (halves spawns even without batching).
4. Add a progress line for the phase and include it in `total_seconds` so the cost is visible in the field.

## Repro

Benchmark harness and artifacts: `/tmp/distill-bench/` (isolated `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_*_DIR`, APFS-cloned brain store, deterministic agent `benchmarks/agent-brain/evidence/distill-perf/local-command-agent.py`). Goroutine dump: `GOTRACEBACK=all` + SIGQUIT \~20s into a run. Brain facts: `architecture.distill.bottleneck`.

## Validated fix (2026-10-19)

`sessionIDsByCheckpoint` (entities_cmd.go:868) passed a nil `*checkpointMetadataCache` to `loadLocalCheckpointSnapshotLocalOnly`, so the provenance join bypassed the export-maintained blob cache (`export/checkpoint-metadata-cache.json.gz`) that the export path and the transcript store already read through. OID resolution is gated on `cache != nil`, so the nil argument also disabled cache lookups downstream.

One-call-site change: load the cache read-only (same pattern as transcript_store.go:233) and pass it.

Same benchmark (git-shim, same template brain, same machine):

|  | before | after |
| -- | -- | -- |
| wall | 82.7s | 17.0s |
| first session done | 67.1s | 2.6s |
| git subprocesses | 4,443 | 53 |
| `git cat-file` calls | \~2,200 | 0 |
| output (facts/chunks/agent calls) | 2590/327/607 | identical |

Focused `internal/cli` tests (Distill/Entit/Provenance/cache/snapshot) pass. Change is uncommitted in the hamburg workspace pending review.

Still open from the candidates list: batched reads (`git cat-file --batch`) for the new-mode transcript path (engine 27.4s vs 15.4s) and the cold `refresh sessions` export (\~2,486 cat-files); progress/timing visibility for pre-engine phases.

## Cache-dependency validation

| patched binary, run | wall | first session done | git cat-file |
| -- | -- | -- | -- |
| metadata cache present (any brain after one export) | 17.0s | 2.6s | 0 |
| metadata cache file deleted | 80.8s | 66.2s | \~2,200 |
| <issue id="8f5bc597-0a46-44ee-8e3a-32609cab134a" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2128/entire-brain-remove-the-local-transcript-cache-read-transcripts-from">COR-2128</issue> checkpoint-backed brain, cache present | 33.0s | 15.0s | 572 (transcript chunks only) |

The speedup depends entirely on `export/checkpoint-metadata-cache.json.gz`. That is safe for the normal flow: distill refuses to run before sessions are exported, and the sessions export loads and saves this cache under the brain write lock (export.go:177-199), so first-time setup pays the blob scan once (in export) and every later distill reads the cache. A missing cache file (pre-cache-era brain, manual deletion) degrades to the old serial scan with identical output.

The remaining 572 cat-files on checkpoint-backed brains are transcript content chunks — the metadata cache does not and should not hold them (that would reintroduce the transcript cache <issue id="8f5bc597-0a46-44ee-8e3a-32609cab134a" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2128/entire-brain-remove-the-local-transcript-cache-read-transcripts-from">COR-2128</issue> removed). Batching via `git cat-file --batch` is the right fix for those and for the export-side first scan.

## Corpus-size sweep (first-run pipeline: `refresh sessions` + first `distill`, truncated checkpoint branch, command agent)

| roots/sessions | A: materialized, pre-fix | B: git-backed, pre-fix | C: git-backed, fixed |

| 250 / 146 | 44.6s | 47.9s | 34.2s |
| 500 / 178 | 79.7s | 83.9s | 54.1s |
| 1,007 / 273 | 153.6s | 168.7s | 106.0s |

On the entire-brain repo (2,095 checkpoints, 273 sessions), a full `entire brain distill --force` spends \~42s of a 57s run before `runDistillForBrain` starts. The user sees the "distill sessions" header and then silence; `--json total_seconds` never includes this time because the timer starts inside the engine.

A goroutine dump 20s into the silent phase shows the main goroutine in:

```
runDistill.func3 (distill_cmd.go:811)
→ newEntityProvenanceResolver
→ loadEntityIndexView → finish() → sessionIDsByCheckpoint
→ loadLocalCheckpointSnapshotLocalOnly → loadLocalCheckpointUnionSnapshot
→ readCheckpointSnapshotMetadata → checkpointBlobReader.read
→ catFileWithPolicy → runCheckpointGitLocal → exec.Cmd.Wait
```

It reads each checkpoint's `metadata.json` blob from `refs/heads/entire/checkpoints/v1` with one `git cat-file` subprocess per blob, each preceded by a `git config -z` subprocess. A git-exec shim measured a flat \~34 reads/s for the whole phase: \~2,200 cat-files, \~4,400 process spawns, \~29ms per serialized read.

## Measurements (2026-10-19, M-series mac, deterministic command agent, jobs 4)

| run | wall | pre-engine | engine (`total_seconds`) | git cat-file calls |
| -- | -- | -- | -- | -- |
| distill, materialized transcripts | 57s | \~42s | 15.4s | \~2,200 |
| distill, checkpoint-backed transcripts (<issue id="8f5bc597-0a46-44ee-8e3a-32609cab134a" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2128/entire-brain-remove-the-local-transcript-cache-read-transcripts-from">COR-2128</issue>) | 76s | \~49s | 27.4s | \~2,772 |
| `refresh sessions` (checkpoint-backed export) | 94s | — | — | \~2,486 |

* The scan repeats on every distill run, warm or cold: the entity-index cache can hit, but `loadEntityIndexView.finish()` re-runs the session join unconditionally.
* <issue id="8f5bc597-0a46-44ee-8e3a-32609cab134a" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2128/entire-brain-remove-the-local-transcript-cache-read-transcripts-from">COR-2128</issue> checkpoint-backed brains pay the same per-blob exec pattern again for transcript reads (engine time 15s → 27s, extraction wait 2.2s → 3.9s) and a third time in `refresh sessions`.
* The phase holds the distill pass lock and emits no progress.
* Released nightly and main perform identically; this is not a regression.

## Fix candidates (impact order)

1. Route checkpoint blob reads through one long-lived `git cat-file --batch` process instead of one exec per blob. The blobs are small JSON; batched, this phase should drop from \~42s to well under a second. Applies to the provenance join, the transcript store, and export alike.
2. Cache the per-checkpoint metadata join keyed by the `entire/checkpoints/v1` tip. Checkpoint content is immutable and content-addressed, so the cache never invalidates mid-branch.
3. Drop the `git config -z` preflight per call (halves spawns even without batching).
4. Add a progress line for the phase and include it in `total_seconds` so the cost is visible in the field.

## Repro

Benchmark harness and artifacts: `/tmp/distill-bench/` (isolated `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_*_DIR`, APFS-cloned brain store, deterministic agent `benchmarks/agent-brain/evidence/distill-perf/local-command-agent.py`). Goroutine dump: `GOTRACEBACK=all` + SIGQUIT \~20s into a run. Brain facts: `architecture.distill.bottleneck`.

## Validated fix (2026-10-19)

`sessionIDsByCheckpoint` (entities_cmd.go:868) passed a nil `*checkpointMetadataCache` to `loadLocalCheckpointSnapshotLocalOnly`, so the provenance join bypassed the export-maintained blob cache (`export/checkpoint-metadata-cache.json.gz`) that the export path and the transcript store already read through. OID resolution is gated on `cache != nil`, so the nil argument also disabled cache lookups downstream.

One-call-site change: load the cache read-only (same pattern as transcript_store.go:233) and pass it.

Same benchmark (git-shim, same template brain, same machine):

|  | before | after |
| -- | -- | -- |
| wall | 82.7s | 17.0s |
| first session done | 67.1s | 2.6s |
| git subprocesses | 4,443 | 53 |
| `git cat-file` calls | \~2,200 | 0 |
| output (facts/chunks/agent calls) | 2590/327/607 | identical |

Focused `internal/cli` tests (Distill/Entit/Provenance/cache/snapshot) pass. Change is uncommitted in the hamburg workspace pending review.

Still open from the candidates list: batched reads (`git cat-file --batch`) for the new-mode transcript path (engine 27.4s vs 15.4s) and the cold `refresh sessions` export (\~2,486 cat-files); progress/timing visibility for pre-engine phases.

## Cache-dependency validation

| patched binary, run | wall | first session done | git cat-file |
| -- | -- | -- | -- |
| metadata cache present (any brain after one export) | 17.0s | 2.6s | 0 |
| metadata cache file deleted | 80.8s | 66.2s | \~2,200 |
| <issue id="8f5bc597-0a46-44ee-8e3a-32609cab134a" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2128/entire-brain-remove-the-local-transcript-cache-read-transcripts-from">COR-2128</issue> checkpoint-backed brain, cache present | 33.0s | 15.0s | 572 (transcript chunks only) |

The speedup depends entirely on `export/checkpoint-metadata-cache.json.gz`. That is safe for the normal flow: distill refuses to run before sessions are exported, and the sessions export loads and saves this cache under the brain write lock (export.go:177-199), so first-time setup pays the blob scan once (in export) and every later distill reads the cache. A missing cache file (pre-cache-era brain, manual deletion) degrades to the old serial scan with identical output.

The remaining 572 cat-files on checkpoint-backed brains are transcript content chunks — the metadata cache does not and should not hold them (that would reintroduce the transcript cache <issue id="8f5bc597-0a46-44ee-8e3a-32609cab134a" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2128/entire-brain-remove-the-local-transcript-cache-read-transcripts-from">COR-2128</issue> removed). Batching via `git cat-file --batch` is the right fix for those and for the export-side first scan.

## Corpus-size sweep (first-run pipeline: `refresh sessions` + first `distill`, truncated checkpoint branch, command agent)

| roots/sessions | A: materialized, pre-fix | B: git-backed, pre-fix | C: git-backed, fixed |
| -- | -- | -- | -- |
| 0 / 0 | 1.4s | 1.0s | 1.2s |
| 250 / 146 | 44.6s | 47.9s | 34.2s |
| 500 / 178 | 79.7s | 83.9s | 54.1s |
| 1,007 / 273 | 153.6s | 168.7s | 106.0s |

Distill phase alone (B → C): 27.0→13.4s, 47.3→17.7s, 96.9→31.5s. Facts identical per size across configs (155/213/326). Worst case (fixed binary, metadata cache deleted, `--force`): 47.3s / 84.2s / 162.7s — degrades to pre-fix behavior. A new user cannot hit the no-cache case: distill requires an export, and export writes the cache. Export is now the dominant first-run phase (\~70% at full size) — the `cat-file --batch` follow-up.

## Post-merge baseline and remaining optimizations

Fix merged in PR #414 / trail 325. New instrumented baseline on main (bab2c681), first cold run, full corpus (1,007 checkpoints / 273 sessions):

| phase | wall | git spawns | cat-file | share |
| -- | -- | -- | -- | -- |
| `refresh sessions` (export) | 98.3s | 5,000 | 2,483 | 72% |
| first distill | 37.9s | 1,171 | 570 | 28% |
| **total** | **136.2s** | **6,171** | **3,053** |  |

Remaining optimizations, in order:

1. **Batch blob reader (export + distill transcript reads).** One long-lived `git cat-file --batch` child per git dir, spawned with the hardened args and `GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1` (same no-egress guarantee as `runCheckpointGitLocal`); `--batch-check` replaces the per-chunk `cat-file -t` existence probes. Route `catFileWithPolicy`, `validateLocalTranscriptSessions`, and `readSnapshotTranscriptFromSource` through it so export, distill, and the transcript store share one implementation. Fall back to per-exec on batch failure.
2. **Amortize the filter-driver probe.** `enumerateRepoFilterDrivers` (`git config -z --get-regexp ^filter\.`) ran 2,501 times during export — once per spawn instead of once per repo/process. Memoize per repoDir.
3. **Reconcile serialization** (9.1s in-engine) — separate, later.

content.text:
Ticket updated. Here's the export analysis:

## What `refresh sessions` (the export) does

It builds the brain's session inventory from git: discover every checkpoint, read each one's metadata, pick the latest transcript per session, verify the transcript blobs exist locally, and write the results. Since COR-2128 it copies **no transcript content** — it only produces:

- `manifest.json` → `sources.sessions` (273 sessions: ids, branches, latest checkpoint, virtual transcript paths)
- `export/checkpoint-metadata-cache.json.gz` (the OID-keyed metadata blob cache)

## How it currently works

1. **Discover sources** — `ls-tree -r` on each checkpoint ref (`entire/checkpoints/v1` local + origin, plus per-checkpoint refs): tree listing + OIDs. A handful of git calls; cheap.
2. **Read metadata** — for each of 1,007 checkpoints, read its `metadata.json` (plus per-session sub-metadata) through `checkpointBlobReader`. On a cold cache every read misses → `catFileWithPolicy` → `runCheckpointGitLocal` → **one `git cat-file -p` subprocess per blob**, serial, on the main goroutine. `GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1` is set per spawn so a partial clone can't phone home (`export.go:680–698`).
3. **Validate transcripts** — `git cat-file -t` per transcript chunk to prove the blob is local (`validateLocalTranscriptSessions`).
4. **Write** manifest + gzip the metadata cache.

## Where the 98.3s goes

| Cost | Measured | Why |
|---|---:|---|
| ~2,483 serial `git cat-file` spawns | ~70–80s | ~30–40ms each; the payload is ~1–3KB of JSON per blob — >95% of each read is process spawn + git startup, not data |
| ~2,501 `git config -z` filter-driver probes | included above | `enumerateRepoFilterDrivers` (the clean/smudge hardening check) runs **once per spawn** instead of once per repo — it doubles the spawn count |
| listings, selection, manifest + cache write | ~10–20s | legitimate work |

Total data actually moved: a few MB. One `git cat-file --batch` process streams that in under a second.

## Proposal

One shared **batch blob reader**, used by export, distill, and the transcript store:

1. Per git dir, spawn one long-lived `git cat-file --batch` child — with the same hardened args (`core.fsmonitor=false`, `core.hooksPath=…`) and `GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1`, so the no-egress guarantee is byte-for-byte the one `runCheckpointGitLocal` enforces today. Requests (`<ref>:<path>`) go in on stdin; `<oid> <type> <size>` + content comes back. A sibling `--batch-check` stream replaces the per-chunk `cat-file -t` probes. "missing" responses map onto the existing promisor-absent error path.
2. Integrate at the existing chokepoint — `catFileWithPolicy`, `validateLocalTranscriptSessions`, `readSnapshotTranscriptFromSource` — so all three consumers (export scan, distill transcript reads, transcript store) collapse with one implementation. Keep the per-exec path as fallback if the batch child dies.
3. Memoize the filter-driver probe per repo dir (it's the cheaper half of the win and worth doing even alone).

Expected: export 98s → ~15–25s, distill 38s → ~22s, cold first run **136s → ~40–50s**. Risks to design around: child lifecycle on context cancel, response size caps (reuse the existing read bounds), and not leaking the child in the long-lived MCP server process.

Want me to start building the batch reader?

content.text:
Correct — it's just the git CLI. `git cat-file --batch` is a built-in mode of plain git: the entire-brain binary spawns **one ordinary git child process** via `os/exec` (exactly like it spawns git today) and keeps it alive, writing object names to its stdin and reading blob contents from its stdout. No MCP, no server, no new dependency — the only change is spawning git once per phase instead of 5,000 times.

The MCP mention was about something else: the entire-brain binary itself can run long-lived (as `entire brain mcp`). In that mode the git child's lifecycle needs owning — kill it when the parent's work is done so it doesn't linger. That's a cleanup detail of the design, not part of the transport.

content.thinking:
I'm designing a batch blob reader using a persistent `git cat-file --batch` subprocess per git directory, with methods to read file contents by ref:path or oid and to check object existence.

For robustness, I want to serialize access with a mutex since the protocol is strictly request/response, and keep lifecycle management simple: lazily spawn child processes in a registry, and if anything goes wrong (error or cancellation), just kill and drop the child so the next call respawns a fresh one rather than trying to recover mid-stream.

For integration, I'm planning to route the local-only path of the existing cat-file policy function through this new batch reader.

I realize the non-local path still uses the CommandRunner abstraction, which tests rely on via fake runners — if I bypass that for the batch process, I'd break test seams that expect specific cat-file invocations. A batch process needs persistent stdin/stdout streaming, which the CommandRunner interface can't express without a larger redesign, so I'm choosing the narrower fix: type-assert for the real ExecRunner and only use the batch path then, falling back to per-exec calls for any fake runner used in tests. That keeps the test seam intact while still giving production the performance benefit.

For the hardened args, I'm checking how the existing ExecRunner already prepends harden config to every git invocation, so the batch child process should apply that same hardening (including the no-lazy-fetch env var) when spawning its cat-file --batch command.

I also want to verify where the filter driver probe gets invoked—if it currently runs once per call, switching to a single long-lived batch process would naturally amortize that cost across many lookups. Memoizing the probe itself could be a worthwhile separate optimization, but I should stay scoped: get the batch reader working first, measure the impact, and only add probe memoization afterward if it's simple and genuinely needed.

For response handling, I need to enforce the existing size caps—since cat-file --batch reports object size upfront, I can check that against the cap before even reading the content. And for testing, I should add a focused test spawning the batch reader against a temporary git repo fixture, covering reading existing and missing objects plus cancellation/respawn behavior, while also rerunning the existing export/transcript tests to make sure nothing regresses.

Before touching shared code, I want to do an impact check on catFileWithPolicy and validateLocalTranscriptSessions — I already traced catFileWithPolicy's four callers (checkpointBlobReader.read, catFile, readSnapshotTranscriptFromSource, readCheckpointSourceTranscript), and I should confirm validateLocalTranscriptSessions' single caller in the transcript store's resolveSnapshot path. I also want to check how runCheckpointGitLocal's envRunner and the ExecRunner type are structured.

Following TDD, I'll write the batch reader alongside its test. My plan is a new file holding a catFileBatch struct that wraps a git cat-file subprocess with its stdin/stdout pipes and a mutex for safe concurrent access, keyed by git directory and mode (batch vs check) in a registry map, with cleanup on read errors to kill and remove the broken entry.

Still designing batch reader...

I need to double-check how hardenedGitArgs and gitNoLazyFetchEnv are defined in runner.go before spawning the subprocess, and also think through edge cases like oversized objects needing to be drained safely and whether paths with embedded newlines could break the batch protocol.

For the existence probe I can reuse `--batch-check` with a separate lightweight child process keyed by gitDir. On the error side, I should map a missing object to something consistent with how `cat-file -p` failures are currently handled, since callers just treat any error as unreadable and wrap it generically -- so I don't need to over-engineer the message format, just keep it clear and respect context cancellation during the read.

Since the batch child persists across requests, I can't fully rely on CommandContext for cancellation mid-stream; I'll check ctx before and after each request and accept that a hung git process gets cleaned up when the parent exits, which is a reasonable simplification for bounded blob sizes. Defining process struct and registry...

Still wiring up the process...

I'm adding a close method that kills the process and removes it from the registry, plus a request method that writes a spec line, reads the response, and marks the process broken on any I/O failure so the caller can clean it up.

I'm now writing a higher-level read function that fetches or creates the shared batch process for a given git directory and locality, reads the object, and drops the process from the registry if it failed—distinguishing a genuinely missing object (a normal, healthy-process error) from an actual I/O break. Then I'm parsing the response header fields to extract the object's metadata.

I'm working through the parsing logic: two fields means "missing" (safe error), three fields means a real object with a size—oversized objects get drained and discarded to avoid desyncing the stream, otherwise the body is read in full along with its trailing newline. Anything ambiguous or unparseable gets treated cautiously, since only a truly confusing response justifies killing the process to prevent corruption, whereas known git responses like "ambiguous" are just normal errors on a still-healthy process. content.text:
# Review PR

Review a pull request with structured, actionable feedback.

## Arguments

- `this` — PR number, URL, or branch name. If empty, review the current branch's open PR.

## Process

### 1. Fetch PR context

```
gh pr view <pr> --json title,body,baseRefName,headRefName,additions,deletions,changedFiles,commits,author
gh pr diff <pr>
```

Read the PR description carefully — it defines scope and intent. Everything you review should be evaluated against what the PR is trying to accomplish.

### 2. Understand the change

Before reviewing line-by-line:
- What is this PR doing and why?
- What files are touched and what's the blast radius?
- Are there any architectural implications?

### 3. Review with this checklist

**Correctness**
- Does the code do what the PR description says?
- Are there logic errors, off-by-one bugs, or unhandled edge cases?
- Are error paths handled correctly?

**Security**
- Any injection risks (SQL, XSS, command injection)?
- Are secrets, tokens, or credentials handled safely?
- Are inputs validated at system boundaries?

**Testing**
- Are there tests for the new/changed behavior?
- Do tests cover edge cases, not just the happy path?
- Are test assertions meaningful (not just "doesn't throw")?

**Design**
- Does the change follow existing codebase patterns and conventions?
- Is the abstraction level appropriate (not over/under-engineered)?
- Are there unnecessary changes outside the stated scope?

**Performance**
- Any N+1 queries, unbounded loops, or missing pagination?
- Are there opportunities for batching or caching that were missed?
- Will this scale with the data sizes it will encounter?

**Readability**
- Are names clear and consistent with the codebase?
- Is complex logic adequately explained?
- Would a future reader understand the "why" behind non-obvious decisions?

### 4. Adversarial review

Take a second, adversarial pass over the diff. Actively try to break the change — assume it has flaws and hunt for them across:

- **Performance** — worst-case inputs, hot paths, allocations, contention.
- **Stability** — race conditions, partial failures, retries, resource leaks, crash recovery.
- **Correctness** — inputs and states that violate the author's assumptions.
- **Simplicity** — code that could be deleted or replaced with something simpler/stdlib.
- **Platform design standards** — deviations from the platform's established design patterns and conventions.

Add any findings to the output using the same severity format.

### 5. Run /simplify

Run the `/simplify` skill (via the Skill tool) against the changed code and fold its findings into the review output.

### 6. Structure your output

For each finding, use this format:

**[severity] file:line — short title**
Description of the issue and why it matters. Include a suggested fix when possible.

Severity levels:
- **[blocking]** — Must fix before merge. Correctness bugs, security issues, data loss risks.
- **[important]** — Should fix. Design problems, missing tests for critical paths, performance issues.
- **[nit]** — Nice to fix. Style, naming, minor improvements. Don't block merge on these.
- **[question]** — Not necessarily wrong, but needs clarification or discussion.

### 7. Summary

End with a brief summary:
- Overall assessment (approve / request changes / needs discussion)
- What the PR does well
- Top 1-3 items that need attention
- Any scope concerns (changes that seem unrelated to the stated goal)

## Guidelines

- Review what's in the diff, not what you wish was there. Don't request unrelated refactoring.
- If the PR is large, focus on the most impactful files first.
- Be specific — "this could be better" is not useful. Show what "better" looks like.
- Distinguish between "this is wrong" and "I would do this differently." Only the former is blocking.
- If you're unsure about something, use [question] severity instead of asserting it's wrong.
- Read relevant source files (not just the diff) when you need context about how changed code integrates with the rest of the system.

Since there's no open PR for the current state and "this" refers to the uncommitted working-tree changes, I'll treat the current diff against HEAD as the review target—the batch reader changes on the compare-distillation-speed branch, whose earlier PR #414 already merged.

My plan: pull the diff across the four touched files, do my own careful adversarial read first, then run the /simplify skill to fold in reuse and cleanup fixes, and finally compile structured findings covering correctness, security, testing, design, performance, and readability.

Going through the implementation adversarially, I'm spotting a likely race: the code checks `p.broken` to decide whether to drop a child process, but that check happens without holding `p.mu`, even though the broader request path does serialize access to the mutex — so this specific flag read looks exposed to a data race.

I'm also weighing whether prefetching transcript reads from multiple goroutines serializes too much on one child's mutex, but the observed extraction_wait numbers still show improvement, so this seems more like a nit than a real bottleneck. I'm also noting that mid-request context cancellation isn't actively checked, which appears intentionally documented behavior, and I'm double-checking whether header parsing handles spec strings with spaces correctly in the batch command.

For the missing-header case, a spec containing a space would break the field count assumption, but since our refs and paths never contain spaces, it's safe in practice. Still, if a space-containing missing spec slipped through, it would produce an extra field that fails size parsing, killing the child and triggering fallback to the per-exec path, which still returns a correct error — so the failure mode is survivable but worth flagging as an edge case to guard against.

On the `fail()` behavior, killing and respawning the child is fine in the batch processor since zombie reaping isn't an issue — normal short-lived children die with the parent, while long-lived MCP children staying alive is expected and documented, so no leak there. I'm also considering whether Windows line-ending differences in git's batch protocol output could affect parsing, since git writes LF even on Windows.

Checking a few other details: the global mutex held during spawn serializes first-use fine, environment inheritance matches the per-exec behavior for test isolation, the 1GiB body guard is equivalent to per-exec buffering, error wrapping with `errors.Is` looks correct, and the `withBody=!check` parameter in `catFileBatchRequest` seems right for the check path.

For `--batch-check` mode, header-only output with no trailing body is correct since `withBody=false` returns before reading the body. The `request` function rejects carriage returns via newline guard, and registry keys on symlinked vs real paths causing duplicate children is harmless. One concern though: the `catFileWithPolicy` fallback to per-exec on batch infrastructure errors could cause doubled costs if batch failures persist — every read would attempt a spawn, fail, then fall back to per-exec.

I'm noting this is pathological but worth flagging. I should add a concurrency test using `go test -race` to catch the race condition identified earlier, running it against concurrent reads. I'm also checking the `transcript_store.go` validate change where `kind != "blob"` relies on `localObjectType` returning a trimmed string, preserving the same error semantics as before for missing objects.

Stderr being nil on the child falls back to per-exec for informative errors, which is clean design. The `for range 3` syntax requires checking the module's Go version, which is 1.27, so that's fine. Now I'm planning to fix the race in (a) and the space guard in (d), then rerun the tests with `-race` to verify before finalizing the review findings.

`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change fixes the root cause at the right depth rather than
patching a symptom with a fragile bandaid. Special cases layered on shared
infrastructure are a sign the fix isn't deep enough — prefer the simpler, more
general change to the underlying mechanism over adding special cases, and name
that change.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

content.thinking:
With four cleanup agents running, I'm doing my own adversarial pass on correctness, security, and testing — the review step the agents were told to skip. I'm flagging a potential data race: p.broken is set under p.mu in request(), but catFileBatchRequest reads it afterward without holding the lock, which could trip the race detector if called concurrently.

The fix is to add a locked isBroken() accessor instead of reading the field directly. I also want to guard against specs containing spaces/tabs/newlines, since a malformed "missing" field can cause a failed ParseInt that kills a healthy child process — better to reject those specs upfront so they fall back to per-exec handling. I should also add a concurrent-read test with -race to catch the race condition directly.

Checking other details: fail() closing and killing under mutex looks fine; the missing-error path through catFileWithPolicy preserves existing error text behavior for callers; there's no shell injection risk since specs are built from controlled ref/path values and the newline guard blocks protocol injection; and PATH lookup via exec.Command matches the existing runner behavior. Since the correctness fixes are mine to make and the other agents are read-only explorers, I'll go ahead and implement (a), (b), and the concurrency test now while they run, accepting they might read pre-fix versions.

I found two real defects during my correctness review: a data race where `catFileBatchRequest` reads `p.broken` without the mutex, and a bug where space-containing specs produce a malformed header that misparses as missing and wrongly kills the child. Fixing both now, with whitespace-containing specs routed to the per-exec path upfront.
